predecessors.name: Aquitaine
predecessors.text: the earlier Aquitaine (Cliopatria row 629-895); the Duchy page's infobox runs the fief 602-late 7th century and 769 to 1453, so the 896-989 gap is Cliopatria's silence

successors.name: Kingdom of France
successors.text: Guyenne and Gascony around Bordeaux, annexed in 1453 ('Aquitaine returned to direct royal rule')

ledger.x: 990: William V begins his rule as duke of Aquitaine and count of Poitou.
990: William V holds the duchy under the French crown.
Page silent on the year: William V 'lost the Loudunais and Mirebalais to Fulk Nerra, count of Anjou' at some point in 990-1030; 1030 (the year he died) is a bound, not a date.
Page silent on the year: William V 'had to give up Confolens, Ruffec, and Chabanais to compensate William II of Angoulême' during 990-1030; 1030 is a bound.
1053: Gascony is joined to Aquitaine under William VIII.
1062: the Duke of Aquitaine takes Saintonge from Anjou.
1098: William IX takes Toulouse.
1122: William IX loses Toulouse.
1137: Eleanor of Aquitaine marries Louis VII and the duchy passes to the French crown.
1137: the duchy stops being a vassal as it passes to the crown.
1204: Eleanor dies and Aquitaine passes to King John, who keeps only the south-west.
1259: the Treaty of Paris gives Henry III Limoges, Cahors and Périgueux.
4 December 1259: the Treaty of Paris makes the duke the king's vassal.
1279: the Agenais passes to the English duke.
19 May 1294: the French Parlement declares the duchy forfeit and France occupies it.
20 May 1303: the Treaty of Paris returns the duchy.
1324: the War of Saint-Sardos strips the duchy of its periphery.
1337: Philip VI reclaims the fief.
1360: the Treaty of Brétigny, ratified at Calais on 24 October 1360, hands Edward III an enlarged Aquitaine.
1362: Edward III makes the Black Prince Prince of Aquitaine.
1369: war resumes over the Brétigny lands.
1377: the English are back around Bordeaux.
1377: the Brétigny lands beyond Gascony and the Bordelais are back with the French crown.
1390: Richard II appoints John of Gaunt Duke of Aquitaine.
1451: Charles VII conquers Guyenne.
1453: Castillon ends the contest.
1453: the duchy is annexed to the French crown.

wars.name: Siege of Barbastro
wars.outcome: William VIII led the allied army that helped Ramiro I of Aragon take the city, killing and enslaving its inhabitants; Aragon lost it again in the following years.

wars.name: Saintonge War
wars.outcome: French victory (infobox); the page has Henry III forced to ask for a five-year truce and a truce signed at Pons on 1 August, both without a year, and no territorial change; Raymond (of Toulouse) was forced to give up Narbonne and Albi.

wars.name: Gascon War
wars.outcome: Philip IV's Parlement declared the fief forfeit on 19 May 1294 and France occupied it; Edward I renounced his vassalage on 24 June 1294; the Treaty of Paris of 20 May 1303 returned the duchy to Edward in exchange for homage.

wars.name: Hundred Years' War
wars.outcome: Philip VI reclaimed the fief in 1337; Brétigny (1360) enlarged the English duchy; war resumed in 1369 and the English were pushed back round Bordeaux by 1377; Castillon (1453) ended English rule.

certainty.note: Feudal frontiers of the High Middle Ages, drawn from regions; no page gives a boundary line.
The Treaty of Paris (4 December 1259) and the Treaty of Amiens (1279) fix the duchy by named provinces and cities; the lines inside them stay approximate.
The 1324 loss rests on the War of Saint-Sardos and the truce of 31 March 1325, which name no provinces; the front of 1337-1359 is not dated on the pages.
The Treaty of Brétigny (1360) fixes the duchy by named provinces; the lines inside them stay approximate.
The frontier moves with the war of 1369-1377 and the French conquest of 1451-1453.
